notes.definition: The poles of a magnet are the places where the magnetic forces are strongest. Every magnet has a north (north-seeking) pole and a south (south-seeking) pole; like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
explanation: A bar magnet has two poles, one at each end. These are the regions where the magnetic force is strongest, which is why iron filings or paper clips cluster at the ends of a bar magnet rather than at the middle. The pole that points towards the Earth's geographic north when the magnet is free to turn is called the north-seeking pole, usually shortened to the north pole (N). The other end is the south pole (S).

When two magnets are brought close together they exert a force on each other. Two like poles (north and north, or south and south) repel each other. Two unlike poles (north and south) attract each other. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact forces: the magnets do not need to touch, because each magnet is in the magnetic field of the other. The forces get weaker as the magnets are moved further apart.

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time. Bar magnets, horseshoe magnets and fridge magnets are permanent magnets. An induced magnet is a material that becomes a magnet only when it is placed in a magnetic field. Magnetic materials, such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt, can have magnetism induced in them. When an iron nail is held near a magnet it becomes an induced magnet and can pick up other nails.

Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction. This is because the end of the induced magnet nearest to the permanent magnet always becomes the opposite pole: a north pole of the permanent magnet induces a south pole in the near end of the iron, and the unlike poles attract. This is why either end of a bar magnet will attract an unmagnetised iron nail, while only one end attracts a particular end of another magnet.

When an induced magnet is removed from the magnetic field it loses most or all of its magnetism quickly. Soft iron loses its magnetism almost completely, which makes it useful for the cores of electromagnets. Steel keeps more of its magnetism, which is why steel is used to make permanent magnets. The only reliable test to show that an object is a permanent magnet is repulsion: attraction could happen with an unmagnetised magnetic material, but repulsion can only happen between two magnets.
keyFacts: The poles of a magnet are where the magnetic forces are strongest.
Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
Magnetic attraction and repulsion are non-contact forces.
A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field.
An induced magnet becomes a magnet only when placed in a magnetic field.
An induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly when removed from the field.
The four magnetic metals are iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
Repulsion is the only sure test that an object is a permanent magnet.

keyTerms.definition: A region of a magnet where the magnetic force is strongest; each magnet has a north pole and a south pole.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time.
A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field and loses most or all of its magnetism when removed.
A material that is attracted to a magnet and can be magnetised: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, such as magnetic, electrostatic and gravitational forces.
A force pushing two objects apart, as between two like magnetic poles.
A force pulling two objects together, as between two unlike magnetic poles or a magnet and a magnetic material.

workedExamples.title: Identifying an unknown pole
workedExamples.question: End X of a bar magnet repels the north pole of a compass needle. Identify the pole at end X and explain your answer.
steps: Repulsion happens only between like poles.
End X repels a north pole, so end X must also be a north pole.
workedExamples.answer: End X is a north pole, because like poles repel.

workedExamples.title: Explaining induced attraction
workedExamples.question: The south pole of a bar magnet is brought near an unmagnetised iron paper clip. Explain why the paper clip is attracted.
steps: The magnet's field induces magnetism in the iron paper clip, which becomes an induced magnet.
The end of the clip nearest the south pole becomes a north pole.
Unlike poles attract, so the clip is pulled towards the magnet.
workedExamples.answer: The clip becomes an induced magnet with a north pole nearest the magnet's south pole, and unlike poles attract.

workedExamples.title: Testing which bar is the magnet
workedExamples.question: You have two identical-looking metal bars. One is a permanent magnet and the other is unmagnetised iron. You also have a labelled bar magnet. Describe how to identify the permanent magnet.
steps: Bring the north pole of the labelled magnet near one end of each bar, then near the other end.
The unmagnetised iron bar is attracted at both ends.
The permanent magnet will repel the north pole at one of its ends (its own north pole).
workedExamples.answer: The bar that repels one pole of the labelled magnet is the permanent magnet.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that all metals are attracted to magnets.
misconceptions.right: In fact only magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel and cobalt) are attracted. Aluminium, copper, gold and brass are not magnetic.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that attraction proves an object is a magnet.
misconceptions.right: In fact a magnet attracts both other magnets and unmagnetised magnetic materials. Only repulsion proves that an object is a permanent magnet.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the magnetic force is strongest in the middle of a bar magnet.
misconceptions.right: In fact the force is strongest at the poles, at the ends of the magnet.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an induced magnet can repel a permanent magnet.
misconceptions.right: In fact induced magnetism always causes attraction, because the near end of the induced magnet always becomes the opposite pole.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think magnets must touch to exert a force.
misconceptions.right: In fact magnetic forces are non-contact forces that act across a gap, getting weaker as the distance increases.

realWorld: Fridge doors use a flexible permanent magnet strip in the seal, which is attracted to the steel cabinet to keep the door closed.
Scrapyards and recycling plants separate steel cans from aluminium cans using magnets, because only the steel cans are attracted.
A compass needle is a small permanent magnet that lines up so its north pole points north.
Magnetic catches on cupboard doors attract a steel plate on the door, using induced magnetism.
examTips: When asked how to show an object is a permanent magnet, always say 'test for repulsion'. Attraction alone gets no credit.
Use the phrase 'non-contact force' when describing magnetic attraction or repulsion; it is a common mark point.
When explaining induced magnetism, state which pole is induced in the near end (the opposite pole) and then link to 'unlike poles attract'.
Name the four magnetic materials precisely: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Do not write 'all metals'.
summary: Magnetic forces are strongest at the poles.
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
Permanent magnets produce their own field; induced magnets need an external field.
Induced magnetism always causes attraction and is quickly lost when the field is removed.
Repulsion is the test for a permanent magnet.

questions.question: Where are the magnetic forces of a bar magnet strongest?
options: In the middle of the magnet
markScheme: 1 mark: At the poles
questions.explanation: The poles, at the ends of a bar magnet, are where the magnetic forces are strongest. Both poles are equally strong; the middle has the weakest effect.

Figure 1 shows two bar magnets. The north poles of the magnets are placed close together.
What happens to the magnets?

markScheme: 1 mark: They repel
questions.explanation: Like poles repel. Two north poles push each other apart.

questions.question: Which of these metals is a magnetic material?
markScheme: 1 mark: Nickel
questions.explanation: The magnetic materials are iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Copper, aluminium and brass are metals but are not attracted to magnets.

questions.question: What type of force acts between two magnets?
markScheme: 1 mark: Non-contact force
questions.explanation: Magnets exert forces on each other without touching, so magnetic forces are non-contact forces.

questions.question: Which statement describes an induced magnet?
options: It produces its own magnetic field at all times
It can only repel other magnets
It becomes a magnet only when placed in a magnetic field
markScheme: 1 mark: It becomes a magnet only when placed in a magnetic field
questions.explanation: An induced magnet becomes magnetic only while it is in a magnetic field. A permanent magnet produces its own field all the time.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the south pole of a bar magnet held near an unmagnetised iron nail.
Which magnetic pole is induced at end X of the nail?

markScheme: 1 mark: North
questions.explanation: The near end becomes the opposite pole, here north, so the nail is attracted. This is why induced magnetism always causes attraction.

questions.question: A student finds that one end of a metal rod is attracted to the north pole of a magnet. What can she conclude?
options: The rod is definitely a permanent magnet
That end of the rod must be a north pole
The rod is made of copper
The rod is either a magnet or a magnetic material
markScheme: 1 mark: The rod is either a magnet or a magnetic material
questions.explanation: Attraction happens between unlike poles and also between a magnet and any magnetic material. So attraction alone cannot show the rod is a permanent magnet.

questions.question: Which material would be best for the core of a temporary magnet that must lose its magnetism quickly when switched off?
markScheme: 1 mark: Soft iron
questions.explanation: Soft iron is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism quickly once the field is removed. Steel keeps its magnetism, so it is used for permanent magnets.

questions.question: End P of rod 1 attracts end Q of rod 2. End P also repels the north pole of a compass. Rod 2 is attracted by both ends of rod 1. What can be concluded?
options: Rod 2 is a permanent magnet and rod 1 is unmagnetised
Rod 1 is a permanent magnet and rod 2 is an unmagnetised magnetic material
markScheme: 1 mark: Rod 1 is a permanent magnet and rod 2 is an unmagnetised magnetic material
questions.explanation: P repels a north pole, so rod 1 is a magnet (P is north). Rod 2 is attracted by both ends of rod 1, so it never shows repulsion: it behaves as an unmagnetised magnetic material with induced magnetism.

questions.question: Why is a steel paper clip that has been held against a magnet for a long time sometimes able to attract other clips after it is removed?
options: Steel keeps some of its induced magnetism
Steel is not a magnetic material
The magnet transferred charge to the clip
markScheme: 1 mark: Steel keeps some of its induced magnetism
questions.explanation: Steel retains some of its magnetism after being magnetised, unlike soft iron which loses almost all of it. This is why steel is used for permanent magnets.

questions.question: State what is meant by a permanent magnet.
markScheme: 1 mark: a magnet that produces its own magnetic field (all the time)
questions.explanation: A permanent magnet does not need an external field to be magnetic; it always has its own magnetic field.

questions.question: Name two metals that are magnetic materials and one metal that is not.
markScheme: 1 mark: any two of iron, steel, nickel, cobalt
1 mark: any non-magnetic metal, such as copper, aluminium, gold, brass
questions.explanation: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Most other metals, such as copper and aluminium, are not attracted to magnets.

1 mark: pair B (south pole near south pole) repel
questions.explanation: Unlike poles attract and like poles repel.

questions.question: Explain why magnetic attraction is described as a non-contact force.
markScheme: 1 mark: the magnets (objects) do not need to touch for the force to act
1 mark: the force acts because each magnet is in the other's magnetic field
questions.explanation: Non-contact forces act across a gap. Magnets attract or repel when separated because the magnetic field of one acts on the other.

questions.question: State what happens to an induced magnet when it is removed from a magnetic field. Give an example of a material that behaves this way.
markScheme: 1 mark: it loses most or all of its magnetism (quickly)
1 mark: (soft) iron
questions.explanation: Induced magnetism depends on the external field. Soft iron loses almost all of it as soon as the field is removed.

questions.question: A student has a bar labelled with an N at one end. She wants to check that the bar really is a permanent magnet. Describe a test she could do and the result that would prove it.
markScheme: 1 mark: bring a known pole (or compass) near the end labelled N
1 mark: if the bar is a magnet, the end labelled N repels a north pole (or the N of a compass needle is pushed away)
1 mark: repulsion is needed because attraction also happens with unmagnetised magnetic material
questions.explanation: Only repulsion proves magnetism, because a magnet also attracts unmagnetised iron or steel.

questions.question: A fridge magnet sticks to a steel fridge door but not to an aluminium window frame. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: steel is a magnetic material and becomes an induced magnet, so it is attracted
1 mark: aluminium is not a magnetic material, so no magnetism is induced
questions.explanation: Magnetism is induced only in magnetic materials. The steel door is attracted; aluminium is unaffected.

questions.question: Explain why either end of a bar magnet will attract an unmagnetised iron nail, but only one end of a bar magnet will attract a particular end of a second bar magnet.
markScheme: 1 mark: the iron nail becomes an induced magnet with the opposite pole nearest the magnet
1 mark: so unlike poles face each other and attraction happens whichever end is used
1 mark: the second bar magnet has fixed poles, so one end of the first magnet is a like pole and repels
questions.explanation: Induced poles always arrange themselves to cause attraction. A permanent magnet's poles are fixed, so one combination of ends gives like poles, which repel.

questions.question: Give one example of where a permanent magnet is used in everyday life.
markScheme: 1 mark: any valid example, such as a compass needle, fridge door seal, fridge magnet or magnetic door catch
questions.explanation: Permanent magnets are used wherever a magnetic force is needed without electricity, such as in compasses and door catches.

questions.question: Which statement about magnetic poles is correct?
options: A magnet can have just one pole
The north pole is always stronger than the south pole
Poles are found only on horseshoe magnets
Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole
markScheme: 1 mark: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole
questions.explanation: Every magnet has two poles, north and south. A magnet cut in half produces two smaller magnets, each with both poles.

markScheme: 1 mark: Only the steel can becomes an induced magnet and is attracted
questions.explanation: Steel is a magnetic material, so magnetism is induced in it and it is attracted. Aluminium is not magnetic, so it is not attracted.

questions.question: Compare permanent magnets and induced magnets.
markScheme: Indicative content: permanent magnets produce their own magnetic field; induced magnets become magnets only when placed in a magnetic field; induced magnets lose most or all of their magnetism quickly when removed; induced magnetism always causes attraction; permanent magnets can attract or repel other magnets; permanent magnets often made of steel, induced magnets often soft iron; both have north and south poles and exert non-contact forces.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison with at least two similarities or differences explained, using correct terms.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one type of magnet, with limited comparison.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A good answer links both types: both have poles and exert non-contact forces, but only permanent magnets have their own field and can repel; induced magnets only attract and quickly lose their magnetism.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows three metal bars, A, B and C, that look identical.
One bar is a permanent magnet, one is unmagnetised iron and one is aluminium.
The student has no other equipment.
Describe how she could identify each bar.
Explain your answer.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif"><rect x="90" y="15" width="240" height="30" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="65" y="35" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">A</text><rect x="90" y="67" width="240" height="30" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="65" y="87" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">B</text><rect x="90" y="119" width="240" height="30" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="65" y="139" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">C</text></svg>

markScheme: Indicative content: bring ends of pairs of bars together; aluminium is not a magnetic material so it is neither attracted nor repelled by any bar; the pair that attracts must be the magnet and the iron; to tell which of these is the magnet, bring the end of one bar to the middle and ends of the other; or try each end against each end of the other: attraction only between magnet and iron, never repulsion with only one magnet; better: hold bar X horizontally and touch the end of bar Y to the middle of X: a magnet's force is weakest in the middle, so if Y is the magnet it still attracts the middle of iron X strongly at its end, whereas if X is the magnet, the end of iron Y is barely attracted by the middle of magnet X; explanation that induced magnetism always attracts, so repulsion cannot be used with only one magnet.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a logical method that identifies all three bars, with clear explanations based on magnetic materials, induced magnetism and the poles being strongest at the ends.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): identifies the aluminium bar and describes a partial method to separate the magnet from the iron with some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as aluminium is not magnetic or magnets attract iron.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Aluminium shows no force with either bar. The magnet and iron always attract, because the iron becomes an induced magnet. Because a magnet's forces are strongest at its poles, the end of the true magnet attracts the middle of the iron bar strongly, but the end of the iron bar is hardly attracted to the middle of the magnet.

questions.question: Explain why an unmagnetised iron nail is attracted to both the north pole and the south pole of a bar magnet.
markScheme: Indicative content: the nail is a magnetic material; in the magnet's field it becomes an induced magnet; near the north pole, the near end of the nail becomes a south pole; near the south pole, the near end becomes a north pole; unlike poles attract in both cases; so induced magnetism always causes attraction.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains induced magnetism and identifies the induced poles in both cases, linked to unlike poles attracting.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that the nail is magnetic or becomes a magnet, with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key idea is that the induced pole at the near end is always opposite to the pole of the magnet, so the force is always attractive.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a magnet hanging from a thread so that it can turn freely.
End X of the magnet is attracted towards end Y of a metal bar.
The bar is turned around so that its other end, Z, faces X. End X is now repelled by end Z.
What is end Z?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif"><line x1="110" y1="5" x2="110" y2="50" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><rect x="40" y="50" width="140" height="26" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="110" y="100" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">magnet</text><text x="192" y="68" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" font-weight="bold">X</text><rect x="250" y="50" width="150" height="26" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="232" y="68" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" font-weight="bold">Y</text><text x="408" y="68" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" font-weight="bold">Z</text><text x="325" y="100" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">metal bar</text><line x1="80" y1="5" x2="140" y2="5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

options: A pole of the opposite type to X
A pole of the same type as X
markScheme: 1 mark: A pole of the same type as X
questions.explanation: Repulsion only happens between like poles, so Z is the same type of pole as X. Y, which attracted X, must be the opposite pole of the second magnet.

questions.question: Suggest why permanent magnets in a compass are made from steel rather than soft iron.
markScheme: 1 mark: steel keeps (retains) its magnetism
1 mark: soft iron would lose its magnetism quickly so the needle would no longer line up with the Earth's field
questions.explanation: A compass needle must remain a magnet permanently. Soft iron is an induced magnet material that loses magnetism quickly.
